questions.q: A support-resolution agent must look up orders, check policy, and draft refunds. Requests follow a predictable sequence. Best architecture?
opts: Fully autonomous agent with 30 tools
Prompt chaining / fixed workflow with tool calls at defined steps
Ten parallel agents voting
One giant prompt with all data inline
questions.exp: Predictable sequence → workflow, not autonomy. The exam repeatedly rewards choosing the simplest sufficient pattern.
why: Thirty tools and full autonomy is far more machinery than a predictable sequence needs.
Correct. A predictable sequence is best served by a fixed workflow with tool calls at defined steps.
Voting multiplies cost for a task with a known path.
Inlining all data ignores the tool calls the task actually requires.

questions.q: When is an orchestrator-workers (multi-agent) pattern justified over a single agent?
opts: Always — more agents, more power
When subtasks are separable, benefit from isolated contexts, or can run in parallel (e.g., broad research)
When latency must be minimal
When you want to save tokens
questions.exp: Multi-agent adds cost and coordination overhead; it pays off for parallelizable, context-heavy, separable work.
why: More agents means more cost, latency, and failure surface, not automatically more capability.
Correct. Separable subtasks that benefit from isolated contexts or parallelism justify the pattern.
Multi-agent designs generally increase latency.
They typically multiply token usage rather than saving it.

questions.q: Your agent loop occasionally spirals, repeating the same failing tool call. The architectural fix is:
opts: Bigger model
Loop guards: max iterations, repeated-failure detection, and an escalation/fallback path
Remove the tool
Retry forever silently
questions.exp: Reliability requires bounded loops with detection of no-progress states and graceful escalation — a core orchestration topic.
why: Capability does not create a termination condition.
Correct. Iteration caps, repeated-failure detection, and an escalation path bound the loop.
Removing capability is disproportionate to a retry bug.
Silent infinite retries are the failure being described.

questions.q: In a routing architecture, an initial classifier sends queries to specialized handlers. The main benefit is:
opts: It eliminates hallucinations
Each handler gets a focused prompt/tools for its category, improving quality and cost per query type
It avoids using the API
Users see more options
questions.exp: Routing = separation of concerns: cheap triage, then specialized focused handling.
why: Routing directs work; it does not make any handler more factual.
Correct. Focused prompts and tools per category improve both quality and cost.
Routing still uses the API for every handler.
Routing is internal; users do not see the branches.

questions.q: An agent must decide between acting autonomously vs. asking the user. Sensitive irreversible actions (deleting data, sending emails) should:
opts: Be fully autonomous for speed
Require human confirmation / approval gates
Be silently logged only
Be disabled entirely always
questions.exp: Checkpoint irreversible or high-blast-radius actions with human-in-the-loop approval.
why: Autonomy on irreversible actions is precisely the risk.
Correct. Irreversible actions need human confirmation before they happen.
Logging detects after the fact; it does not prevent.
A blanket ban removes legitimate capability rather than governing it.

questions.q: Your team wants consistent Claude Code behavior across all engineers on a repo. Best mechanism?
opts: Verbal team norms
A checked-in CLAUDE.md with conventions, commands, and guardrails
Each dev's private notes
Longer chat sessions
questions.exp: CLAUDE.md in the repo gives every session the same project context — the canonical Claude Code workflow answer.
why: Verbal norms are neither discoverable nor enforceable.
Correct. A checked-in instructions file applies the same conventions to everyone.
Private notes guarantee divergence between engineers.
Session length has nothing to do with shared conventions.

questions.q: For a large refactor, the recommended Claude Code workflow is:
opts: One giant 'refactor everything' prompt
Plan first (explore/plan mode), review the plan, then execute in steps with verification (tests) between
Disable tests to go faster
Let it run unattended overnight
questions.exp: Explore → plan → execute → verify. Plan-then-act with test checkpoints is the tested best practice.
why: A single sweeping instruction produces an unreviewable change.
Correct. Plan, review the plan, then execute in verified steps.
Tests are the verification that makes agentic changes safe.
Unattended overnight runs remove the review the workflow depends on.

questions.q: Claude Code subagents are useful primarily because they:
opts: Are cheaper per token
Run tasks in separate context windows, keeping the main session focused and enabling parallel work
Have different training data
Skip permissions
questions.exp: Subagents isolate context per task — the main thread stays clean and work can fan out.
why: Token pricing does not differ by subagent.
Correct. Separate context windows keep the main session focused and enable parallel work.
Subagents share the same underlying models.
Permissions still apply to subagents.

questions.q: To let Claude Code run repository tests automatically before declaring work done, you would:
opts: Trust it remembers
Encode the requirement in CLAUDE.md and/or use hooks to run tests on completion
Run tests manually a week later
Avoid tests in agentic workflows
questions.exp: Instructions in CLAUDE.md plus hooks make verification systematic instead of hopeful.
why: Relying on recall is not a mechanism.
Correct. Encode the requirement in project instructions, or enforce it with hooks.
Delayed manual testing defeats the point of an automatic gate.
Tests matter more in agentic workflows, not less.

questions.q: An extraction pipeline needs machine-parseable output with exact fields. The architect's choice:
opts: Free-form text and a regex parser
Schema-constrained structured output (or a tool with strict input schema), validated downstream
Ask for 'mostly JSON'
Markdown tables
questions.exp: Contract-first: define the schema, constrain generation to it, validate anyway. Prompt Engineering & Structured Output is a CCAR-F domain.
why: Regex over free text is the fragile pattern this replaces.
Correct. Constrain generation to a schema, and validate downstream regardless.
'Mostly JSON' is not a contract anything can rely on.
Markdown tables are for humans, not machine parsing.

questions.q: A prompt performs well on easy inputs but fails on edge cases. Best improvement strategy?
opts: Add few-shot examples covering the failing edge cases and explicit rules for them
Make the prompt shorter
Raise temperature
Switch providers
questions.exp: Targeted examples of hard cases are the highest-leverage prompt fix — they teach the boundary behavior.
why: Correct. Show the failing cases as examples and state the rule for them.
Removing content is unlikely to add the missing guidance.
Sampling parameters are rejected on current models and never fixed edge cases.
Provider choice does not address an under-specified prompt.

questions.q: For a multi-pass review loop (draft → critique → revise), the main architectural benefit is:
opts: Fewer tokens used
Quality gains from self-review catching errors a single pass misses
It removes the need for tests
Faster responses
questions.exp: Evaluator/reviser loops trade tokens for quality — appropriate when output quality justifies the cost.
why: Multi-pass review costs more tokens, not fewer.
Correct. A critique pass catches errors that a single generation misses.
Self-review is not a substitute for tests.
Extra passes increase latency.

questions.q: You need Claude's response to be valid JSON matching a fixed schema. On current Claude models, the correct mechanism is:
opts: Prefilling the assistant turn with "{" so generation continues as JSON
Structured outputs — a schema via output_config.format, or a tool with a strict input schema
Asking for JSON in the system prompt and repairing the output with a regex
Setting a stop sequence at "}" and retrying on parse failures
questions.exp: Structured outputs constrain generation to your schema, so the response is valid by construction. Prefilling the assistant turn is the older trick and now returns a 400 error on current Claude models.
why: Assistant-turn prefill returns an error on current Claude models.
Correct. Structured outputs constrain generation to the schema.
Prompt-and-repair is the failure-prone pattern this replaces.
Stop sequences end generation; they do not enforce a shape.

questions.q: You're designing tools for an agent. Which principle applies?
opts: Many overlapping micro-tools are best
Few, well-named, clearly documented tools with distinct purposes and strict schemas
Tools should share one generic 'do_anything' endpoint
Descriptions waste tokens
questions.exp: Overlapping or vague tools cause wrong selections. Distinct, well-documented tools are an exam staple.
why: Overlapping micro-tools multiply selection errors.
Correct. Few, distinct, well-documented tools with strict schemas.
A generic catch-all endpoint destroys the model's ability to choose correctly.
Descriptions are what drive correct selection; they earn their tokens.

questions.q: A tool can return 10,000 rows. The agent only ever needs a handful. Design the tool to:
opts: Return everything for completeness
Support filtering/pagination and return concise, relevant results to protect the context window
Return a file path only
Fail if results exceed 100
questions.exp: Token-efficient tool responses are an architectural responsibility — context is a scarce resource.
why: Returning everything wastes context and buries the relevant rows.
Correct. Filtering and pagination let the agent request only what it needs.
A bare path forces another step to read the data.
Hard failure on large results makes the tool unusable for legitimate queries.

questions.q: When should you wrap a capability as an MCP server instead of a bespoke in-app tool?
opts: Never — MCP is only for Anthropic products
When multiple clients/agents should reuse it through a standard interface
Only for databases
When you need lower latency than function calls
questions.exp: MCP shines for reuse and interoperability across clients; bespoke tools are fine for single-app needs.
why: MCP is an open standard, not product-specific.
Correct. Reuse across multiple clients or agents is what justifies the interface.
It is not limited to databases.
A protocol hop does not beat an in-process call on latency.

questions.q: An MCP server exposes a 'run_sql' tool for analytics. The safest design is:
opts: Full read-write on production
Read-only access to a replica, query allowlists/limits, and audit logging
Root credentials for flexibility
No limits — the model is careful
questions.exp: Least privilege + read-only replicas + auditability: tool design is security design.
why: Production read-write through a model-callable tool is the widest possible blast radius.
Correct. Read-only replica, allowlists and limits, and audit logging.
Root credentials remove every meaningful control.
Relying on model carefulness is not a security control.

questions.q: A long-running agent gradually forgets early constraints. Architectural mitigation?
opts: Hope for the best
Compaction: periodically summarize state/decisions into a durable note re-injected into context
Restart and lose everything
Raise temperature
questions.exp: Context compaction / structured note-taking preserves critical state past window limits — core Context Management material.
why: Hope is not a mitigation.
Correct. Compact state and decisions into a durable note that is re-injected.
Restarting discards everything learned.
Sampling parameters are rejected on current models and are unrelated to context loss.

questions.q: Which is a signal you should retrieve context just-in-time rather than preload everything?
opts: Corpus far exceeds the context window and most content is irrelevant per query
The corpus is 2 pages
Latency doesn't matter
You enjoy large bills
questions.exp: Just-in-time retrieval (search/RAG, agentic file exploration) beats exhaustive preloading for large corpora.
why: Correct. A corpus far larger than the window, mostly irrelevant per query, is the retrieval case.
A two-page corpus fits trivially and needs no retrieval.
Latency tolerance does not argue for or against retrieval.
Cost indifference is not an engineering signal.

questions.q: To make an agent pipeline resilient to a model outage or degraded responses, an architect plans:
opts: Nothing — outages are rare
Fallbacks: retries with backoff, model fallback tiers, circuit breakers, and graceful degradation paths
A status page
Blaming the vendor
questions.exp: Reliability domain: design for failure with retries, fallbacks, and degradation modes.
why: Outages are routine at scale and must be designed for.
Correct. Retries with backoff, fallback tiers, circuit breakers, and graceful degradation.
A status page reports failure; it does not survive it.
Attribution is not a resilience strategy.

questions.q: Where should deterministic logic (date math, exact totals, ID validation) live in an agentic system?
opts: In the model's prompt as instructions
In code/tools — let the model orchestrate, let code compute
In the model's memory
Nowhere
questions.exp: Models orchestrate and interpret; deterministic computation belongs in code for correctness — a recurring architecture principle.
why: Instructions cannot make arithmetic deterministic.
Correct. Let code compute exact values and let the model orchestrate.
There is no durable memory that performs computation.
The logic still has to exist somewhere.

questions.q: Two agents in your system communicate by passing entire conversation histories to each other. Costs explode. Better pattern?
opts: Pass distilled, structured summaries/artifacts between agents instead of raw transcripts
Bigger context windows
Compress with zip
Merge into one agent with double context
questions.exp: Inter-agent handoffs should exchange minimal structured state, not full transcripts.
why: Correct. Pass distilled structured artifacts rather than raw transcripts.
A larger window raises the ceiling without addressing the waste.
Compression does not help content that must be read as tokens.
Merging discards the isolation that motivated the split.

questions.q: You need consistent tone/policy across 40 different prompts in a product. The maintainable approach is:
opts: Copy-paste the policy into each prompt
A shared, versioned system-prompt component included by all prompts
Trust each author
Fine-tune per prompt
questions.exp: Treat prompts like code: shared components, versioning, and review keep 40 prompts coherent.
why: Copy-paste guarantees the 40 copies drift apart.
Correct. One shared, versioned component included everywhere.
Author discretion is what produces inconsistency.
Fine-tuning per prompt is disproportionate and unmaintainable.

questions.q: A CI pipeline uses Claude Code headlessly to fix lint errors on PRs. Critical safeguard?
opts: No safeguards; speed matters
Scoped permissions, no push to main, changes land as PR diffs a human reviews
Auto-merge everything green
Run as repo admin
questions.exp: Headless agent + CI = least privilege and human review of diffs. Claude Code for CI is one of the six exam scenarios.
why: Unsupervised changes with no gate is the risk itself.
Correct. Scoped permissions, no direct push, and human-reviewed PR diffs.
Auto-merge removes the review that makes this safe.
Admin rights give the widest possible blast radius.

questions.q: Claude keeps calling a search tool when it should use the calculator. First fix to try?
opts: Delete the search tool
Sharpen both tool descriptions to state exactly when each should (and shouldn't) be used
Fine-tune the model
Add a third tool
questions.exp: Tool-selection errors usually trace to ambiguous descriptions — clarify boundaries and add usage notes.
why: Deleting a needed tool to fix a selection problem loses capability.
Correct. Selection errors are usually description problems — state when each applies and when it does not.
Fine-tuning is a heavyweight answer to an ambiguous description.
A third tool adds another option to confuse.

questions.q: A task decomposes into four independent research questions whose answers are combined at the end. The fitting pattern is:
opts: A single sequential chain
Orchestrator with parallel workers, then a synthesis step
A router that picks one question
A human performing each step
questions.exp: Independent subtasks that recombine is the orchestrator-workers shape; parallelism is the whole benefit.
why: Sequential execution wastes the independence between the questions.
Correct. Fan out independent work, then synthesize the results.
Routing picks one path; here all four answers are needed.
Manual execution discards the automation entirely.

questions.q: Requests fall into three distinct categories, each best handled by a different prompt and model. The right pattern is:
opts: Run all three handlers and pick the best output
A routing step that classifies then dispatches to the specialist handler
One general prompt covering all three
A multi-agent debate
questions.exp: Routing classifies once and dispatches, which keeps each handler focused and avoids paying for work you discard.
why: Running everything triples cost to use one result.
Correct. Classify, then dispatch to the specialist path.
A single generic prompt underperforms specialists on all three.
Debate adds cost and latency without addressing categorization.

questions.q: The strongest argument for choosing a simpler orchestration than you think you need is:
opts: Simpler systems are always more accurate
Every added layer adds cost, latency, and failure surface, and must earn its place
Complex systems are harder to explain to customers
Simple systems use newer models
questions.exp: Published guidance is explicit: use the simplest pattern that works and escalate only when the task demands it.
why: Simplicity is not automatically more accurate; it is cheaper to operate and reason about.
Correct. Complexity has real operational cost and must be justified.
Explicability matters but is not the core engineering argument.
Model choice is independent of orchestration complexity.

questions.q: A pipeline has a step whose output quality varies and materially affects everything downstream. The best structural addition is:
opts: Run the step twice and keep the longer output
An evaluator step that checks the output against criteria and triggers a retry or escalation
Skip the step when it is slow
Ask the user to check it
questions.exp: Evaluator-optimizer inserts a quality gate exactly where variance is costly, with a defined remedy.
why: Length is not a quality criterion.
Correct. Gate the variable step with explicit criteria and a defined remedy.
Skipping a load-bearing step trades quality for speed silently.
Pushing verification onto users does not scale.

questions.q: The clearest sign an orchestration has become too complex is:
opts: It uses more than one model
Failures are hard to attribute to a specific step, and changes have unpredictable effects
It has more than three prompts
It costs more than last month
questions.exp: Diagnosability is the practical limit. When you cannot localize a failure, you can no longer safely change the system.
why: Multiple models is normal right-sizing.
Correct. Loss of attribution and predictability is the real complexity ceiling.
Prompt count alone is not a meaningful threshold.
Cost growth may be legitimate; it is not itself a complexity signal.

questions.q: The main reason to commit a project-level instructions file for Claude Code is:
opts: It makes the model faster
Conventions, commands, and constraints apply consistently for everyone on the repository
It replaces code review
It stores API keys conveniently
questions.exp: Checked-in project instructions make agent behavior a reviewable, shared property of the repository rather than per-developer folklore.
why: Instructions do not affect inference speed.
Correct. Shared, versioned conventions apply to every contributor.
Automated assistance does not remove human review.
Secrets must never be committed.

questions.q: Running an agentic coding workflow in CI, the most important guardrail is:
opts: Giving it the largest model
Scoping what it may change and requiring review before anything merges
Letting it run without a time limit
Disabling tests to avoid false failures
questions.exp: In CI the agent operates unattended, so blast radius and merge gates are what keep it safe.
why: Capability does not bound what the agent may alter.
Correct. Constrain scope and keep a human merge gate.
Unbounded runs are a cost and reliability hazard.
Disabling tests removes the signal you most need.

questions.q: A coding agent makes a sweeping refactor when a narrow fix was wanted. The most effective correction is:
opts: Use a smaller model
State the scope explicitly — which files may change and what must not — and ask for the minimal diff
Run it again and hope
Accept the refactor
questions.exp: Scope is an instruction. Unstated boundaries are the usual cause of over-broad changes.
why: Capability is not the issue; specification is.
Correct. Name the allowed scope and ask for the smallest change that works.
Repetition without new constraints reproduces the behavior.
Accepting an unrequested refactor inherits unreviewed risk.

questions.q: The best first step when adopting agentic coding on a large legacy codebase is:
opts: Ask it to modernize everything at once
Start with well-tested, well-bounded areas where correctness is verifiable quickly
Disable the test suite for speed
Give it write access to production
questions.exp: Verifiability is what makes agentic changes safe. Start where tests can tell you immediately whether the change was right.
why: Wholesale modernization is unreviewable and high risk.
Correct. Begin where verification is fast and the blast radius is small.
Tests are the verification mechanism; removing them removes safety.
Production write access is never an appropriate starting point.

questions.q: Version-controlling the prompts and instructions that drive a coding workflow matters mainly because:
opts: It reduces token usage
Behavior changes become reviewable and revertible like any other change
It is required by the tool
It makes onboarding slower
questions.exp: Prompts are executable configuration. Treating them as code gives you review, history, and rollback.
why: Version control does not change token consumption.
Correct. Review, history, and rollback apply to behavior-defining text.
It is a practice, not a product requirement.
Shared, versioned conventions speed onboarding up.

questions.q: Designing a contract between an extraction step and its consumer, the right order is:
opts: Write the prompt, see what comes out, then write a parser
Define the schema first, constrain generation to it, and validate downstream anyway
Ask for markdown and parse headings
Let each consumer parse differently
questions.exp: Contract-first design removes parse failures by construction, and validation still guards semantics.
why: Reverse-engineering a contract from observed output is fragile.
Correct. Schema first, constrained generation, and validation regardless.
Prose formats are not machine contracts.
Divergent parsers multiply failure modes.

questions.q: A schema-constrained step returns structurally valid output with a nonsensical value. This shows that:
opts: Structured outputs are unreliable
Schemas guarantee shape, not meaning — semantic validation is still required
The schema was too strict
The model needs replacing
questions.exp: Shape and meaning are different guarantees. Constrained decoding delivers the first; your validation must cover the second.
why: The mechanism worked exactly as specified.
Correct. Shape conformance is not semantic correctness.
Strictness produced valid structure; it was never a meaning check.
Every model can emit schema-valid nonsense.

questions.q: Across many documents you need identical structure. Beyond a schema, the most useful addition is:
opts: A longer system prompt
One or two worked examples showing the structure filled in for edge cases
A higher effort level on every call
Randomizing the prompt to avoid overfitting
questions.exp: Examples communicate expectations that a schema cannot express, particularly around edge cases and conventions.
why: Length without specificity does not improve consistency.
Correct. Worked examples pin down conventions the schema cannot encode.
More reasoning does not supply missing conventions.
Deliberate variation undermines consistency.

questions.q: The most reliable way to evolve a prompt that many systems depend on is:
opts: Edit it in place and watch for complaints
Version it, run the change against a regression set, and roll out behind a gate
Only change it during quiet periods
Let each team keep a copy
questions.exp: Shared prompts are shared infrastructure. Versioning plus evals plus staged rollout is the safe change path.
why: Complaint-driven detection is slow and damaging.
Correct. Version, evaluate against fixed cases, and gate the rollout.
Timing does not reduce the risk of an unmeasured change.
Forked copies guarantee divergence.

questions.q: When a task needs both prose for humans and fields for a system, the cleanest design is:
opts: Ask for prose and regex the fields out
Define one schema containing both the structured fields and a prose field
Run the task twice with different prompts
Ask for prose and let each consumer interpret it
questions.exp: A single schema covering both consumers keeps them in sync and avoids a second, divergent generation.
why: Regex over prose is the fragility structured outputs exist to remove.
Correct. One schema, both consumers, generated once and consistent.
Two runs can disagree with each other.
Unstructured interpretation produces inconsistent downstream behavior.

questions.q: Designing a tool an agent will call unsupervised, the most important property is:
opts: A short name
Narrow scope with clearly described preconditions and failure modes
Returning as much data as possible
Accepting free-form text arguments
questions.exp: Unsupervised tools should be narrow and legible: easy to select correctly, hard to misuse, and clear when they fail.
why: Names matter less than described behavior.
Correct. Narrow scope and explicit contracts make selection and recovery reliable.
Oversized responses waste context and bury the relevant part.
Free-form arguments invite malformed calls.

questions.q: Two tools have overlapping purposes and the agent frequently picks the wrong one. The best fix is:
opts: Delete one arbitrarily
Clarify the descriptions so each states when to use it and when not to, or merge them
Add a third tool to choose between them
Rename them to be similar
questions.exp: Selection errors are usually description problems. State the boundary explicitly, or remove the ambiguity by merging.
why: Arbitrary removal may drop needed capability.
Correct. Make the boundary explicit, or eliminate it by merging.
A meta-tool adds a layer without resolving the ambiguity.
Similar names make confusion more likely.

questions.q: A tool returns 5,000 rows when the agent needs a handful. The right change is:
opts: Increase the context window
Add pagination and filtering parameters so the agent requests only what it needs
Summarize the rows with another model call
Accept it as the cost of completeness
questions.exp: Tool design should let the caller narrow the result. Filtering at the source beats paying to carry and then discard data.
why: Larger windows postpone the problem at higher cost.
Correct. Give the agent parameters to narrow the request at the source.
An extra call to fix an oversized payload adds cost and latency.
Uncontrolled payloads degrade both cost and reasoning quality.

questions.q: Exposing internal capabilities through MCP rather than a bespoke integration is most justified when:
opts: Only one client will ever use them
Multiple clients or agents need the same capabilities, now or plausibly later
The team wants to try a new protocol
The capabilities are trivial
questions.exp: MCP's value is reuse across clients. With a single permanent consumer, the abstraction may not pay for itself.
why: A single consumer rarely justifies the extra indirection.
Correct. Reuse across clients is what the standard buys you.
Novelty is not an architectural reason.
Triviality argues against added protocol machinery.

questions.q: A tool performs an irreversible external action. The architecture should:
opts: Rely on the agent's judgment
Require explicit confirmation, and make the operation idempotent or safely retryable where possible
Retry automatically on any error
Log the action and move on
questions.exp: Irreversible actions need a gate before, and idempotency so that retries after ambiguity do not double-apply.
why: Judgment is not a control for irreversible effects.
Correct. Confirm before acting, and design for safe retries.
Blind retries on an irreversible action can duplicate it.
Logging is detection after the fact, not prevention.

questions.q: An agent's context fills during a long task. The right design response is:
opts: Truncate the oldest messages automatically
Compact — summarize decisions and state into a durable note, re-injected as the working record
Start over with a fresh session
Move to a model with a larger window and change nothing else
questions.exp: Compaction preserves meaning rather than position. Blind truncation drops whatever happens to be oldest, including load-bearing constraints.
why: Truncation discards by position, not importance.
Correct. Summarize the decisions and state that must survive.
Restarting loses everything learned.
A larger window delays the same failure without addressing it.

questions.q: The most reliable way to keep critical constraints in force across a long run is:
opts: State them once at the very start
Carry them in a durable structure that is re-injected each cycle
Repeat them in every user message manually
Rely on the model remembering
questions.exp: Constraints that must hold throughout belong in state that is deliberately re-supplied, not in a single early message.
why: Early statements get crowded out as the run grows.
Correct. Re-inject the constraints as part of the working record.
Manual repetition does not scale and is easily forgotten.
There is no persistence across context loss.

questions.q: An agent occasionally repeats the same failing action indefinitely. The right safeguard is:
opts: A longer system prompt
Repeated-failure detection with a cap, then escalation to a different strategy or a human
A larger context window
Removing the tool
questions.exp: Loop detection with a defined escalation converts an infinite retry into a bounded, reportable outcome.
why: Instructions do not enforce termination.
Correct. Detect repetition, cap it, and escalate deliberately.
More context does not stop a behavioral loop.
Removing capability is disproportionate to a retry bug.

questions.q: Retrieved context and the agent's own conclusions should be distinguished because:
opts: It improves formatting
Conflating sourced facts with generated inferences makes errors impossible to trace
It reduces token usage
The API requires it
questions.exp: Traceability depends on knowing what came from a source and what the system concluded. Blurring them destroys auditability.
why: This is an auditability concern, not presentation.
Correct. Separating sourced from inferred keeps errors traceable.
Labeling provenance does not reduce tokens.
This is a design practice, not an API requirement.

questions.q: The best reliability metric for a long-running agent is:
opts: Average tokens per run
The rate of runs that reach a correct, verifiable end state — with partial progress measured separately
Number of tool calls
Total wall-clock time
questions.exp: Outcome correctness is the metric that matters; token and step counts are diagnostics, not goals.
why: Token usage is a cost signal, not a reliability one.
Correct. Verified end-state success, with partial progress tracked separately.
Tool-call volume says nothing about whether the task succeeded.
Duration matters operationally but does not measure correctness.

questions.q: Two agents in a workflow disagree about a fact drawn from different retrieved passages. The right architectural response is:
opts: Let the later agent overwrite the earlier conclusion
Surface the conflict with both sources attached, and resolve it by a defined precedence rule or human judgment
Average the two answers
Retry until they agree
questions.exp: Silent overwrites hide contradictions in the source material. Conflicts should be made visible and resolved by an explicit rule.
why: Recency is not authority; the earlier conclusion may be the correct one.
Correct. Surface the conflict with provenance and apply a defined precedence rule.
Averaging facts is meaningless and can produce a claim neither source supports.
Retrying until agreement selects for luck, not truth.

cards.f: What CCAR-F study domains does this app use?
cards.b: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration · Claude Code Workflows · Prompt Eng & Structured Output · Tool Design & MCP · Context Mgmt & Reliability. These are this app's study groupings — official weightings are in the Partner Academy exam guide.

$125 USD (confirmed on Anthropic's Pearson VUE page). Independent study sites widely report 120 minutes, scenario-based and a scaled pass mark of 720 on a 100–1000 range, but Anthropic publishes the authoritative format only in the Partner Academy exam guide — treat those figures as unconfirmed.

Customer Support Agent · Code Gen with Claude Code · Multi-Agent Research · Developer Productivity · Claude Code for CI · Structured Data Extraction. Useful practice contexts for architect-level thinking — not a verified list of exam scenarios.
Use the simplest pattern that works: prompt → workflow → single agent → multi-agent. Escalate complexity only when the task demands it.
Prompt chaining · Routing · Parallelization (sectioning/voting) · Orchestrator-workers · Evaluator-optimizer
Max iterations, repeated-failure detection, budget caps, and escalation paths — how agents avoid spiraling.
Summarizing conversation/agent state into a durable structured note when nearing context limits, then continuing with the summary.
Delegated tasks running in separate context windows — isolation keeps the main thread clean; enables parallelism.
Scripted actions that fire at lifecycle points (e.g., after edits, before completion) — enforce tests/lint deterministically.
Distinct purpose · precise description with when-to-use · strict input schema · concise token-efficient output · safe failure messages
Human confirmation required before irreversible/high-impact actions (deletes, sends, payments, prod changes).
Deterministic logic (math, validation, exact lookups) belongs in tools/code; the model decides and interprets.

lessons.b:
Architect Foundations assumes you're comfortable with everything in the Developer cert — the Messages API, tool use, the basic agent loop, and MCP at a conceptual level. If those feel shaky, it's worth a detour through the Developer study guide first. What's new here is the shift in vantage point: instead of 'how do I write the code for one agent,' the question becomes 'given a business problem, what's the right shape of system, and why.'

The architect's core question

Every scenario in this cert is really asking the same thing in different clothes: what is the simplest system that reliably solves this problem, and where exactly does it become unreliable? Architecture is fundamentally about trade-offs — more orchestration buys capability but costs latency, money, and new failure modes; less orchestration is cheap and fast but breaks on anything the fixed path didn't anticipate. Good architects can articulate exactly where that line sits for a given problem, not just default to 'more agents' or 'fewer agents.'

A note on scenario-based study

Architect-level questions tend to arrive wrapped in a business scenario — customer support agents, code generation with Claude Code, multi-agent research, developer productivity, CI pipelines, structured data extraction. The same underlying knowledge — orchestration patterns, tool design, context management — gets tested through different business framings, so learning the patterns deeply matters far more than memorizing any one scenario. For the actual exam format, see the official exam guide in Partner Academy.

Key takeaways
  • This cert assumes Developer-level fluency with the API, tools, and basic agents.
  • Every scenario reduces to: what's the simplest reliable architecture, and where does it break?
  • The same core patterns repeat across all 6 possible exam scenarios — learn patterns, not scenarios.

Architecture here means choosing the shape of the system, and Anthropic's own guidance is explicit: use the simplest pattern that works, and escalate complexity only when the task demands it. Every additional layer adds cost, latency, and failure surface.

Climb this ladder only as far as the task actually requires.

The patterns, simplest first

  • Single call — one well-specified request. Most tasks stop here.
  • Prompt chaining / fixed workflow — known steps in a known order, with tool calls at defined points. The right answer for predictable sequences such as look up order, check policy, draft refund.
  • Routing — a classifier dispatches to specialist handlers. Each handler gets a focused prompt and tool set, improving quality and cost per query type.
  • Evaluator-optimiser — a generate step plus a check step with defined criteria and a retry or escalation path. Use where one step's quality varies and everything downstream depends on it.
  • Orchestrator-workers — separable subtasks explored in parallel, then synthesised. Justified when subtasks are genuinely independent and benefit from isolated contexts.

Autonomy is a spectrum, not a switch

An agent decides its own steps; a workflow follows yours. Sensitive or irreversible actions — deleting data, sending mail, moving money — require human confirmation regardless of how autonomous the surrounding system is. Autonomy is about who chooses the path, never about who approves consequences.

Bounding loops

Agent loops occasionally spiral, repeating a failing action indefinitely. The architectural fix is loop guards: maximum iterations, repeated-failure detection, budget caps, and an escalation or fallback path. A more capable model does not create a termination condition, and removing the tool is disproportionate to a retry bug.

Knowing when it is too complex

The practical ceiling is diagnosability. When failures can no longer be attributed to a specific step, and changes have unpredictable effects, the system has outgrown its design — regardless of how many models or prompts it happens to use.

Picking the pattern
Predictable sequence, tools at known points -> fixed workflow
Three query types, different handling       -> routing
One variable step gates everything after it -> evaluator-optimiser
Four independent research questions         -> orchestrator-workers
Steps unknowable until run time             -> agent loop + guards
Key takeaways
  • Use the simplest pattern that works; escalate only on demonstrated need.
  • Fixed workflows beat agents whenever the path is predictable.
  • Routing gives each category a focused prompt and tool set.
  • Irreversible actions need human confirmation at any autonomy level.
  • Loop guards — caps, failure detection, budgets, escalation — are mandatory.
  • Loss of failure attribution is the real complexity ceiling.
Common pitfalls

Reaching for multi-agent first. More agents means more cost, latency, and failure surface — not automatically more capability.

Voting or debating on a task with a known path. It multiplies cost to reach an answer a workflow would have produced directly.

🎯 Exam Tip — Workflow vs Agent Loop Selection

Predictable multi-step tasks belong in fixed, deterministic workflows. Use autonomous agent loops only when the execution path genuinely cannot be known in advance.

Multi-Agent Architectures: Router (single delegate selection) vs Orchestrator-Worker (parallel subagents recombined).

Topological Choice Matrix

Architecture When to Use Cost & Latency Impact
Deterministic Pipeline Known, predictable sequence of steps Lowest cost, lowest latency, highest reliability
Router Agent Classify request into 1 of N specialist handlers Low cost (single routing step + 1 handler)
Orchestrator-Workers Task breaks into independent subtasks run in parallel Higher token cost, parallel speed, subagent isolation

Agentic coding is structured work, not a single sweeping instruction. The architect's job is to make the agent's behaviour consistent across a team, bounded in what it may change, and verifiable before anything merges.

The recommended Claude Code loop for non-trivial changes — verify gates every execute step.

Project instructions as shared configuration

A checked-in project instructions file — conventions, commands, guardrails — applies the same rules to every engineer on the repository. Verbal norms are neither discoverable nor enforceable, and private notes guarantee divergence. Because it is committed, it is reviewable and revertible like any other change. Secrets never belong in it.

Plan, then execute in verified steps

For anything substantial, explore and plan first, review the plan, then execute in steps with verification — tests — between them. A single 'refactor everything' prompt produces an unreviewable change. Tests are the mechanism that makes agentic edits safe, so disabling them to move faster removes the only signal that matters.

Scope is an instruction

When an agent makes a sweeping change where a narrow fix was wanted, the usual cause is that no boundary was stated. Say which files may change, what must not, and ask for the minimal diff. Unstated scope is inferred scope.

Subagents

Subagents run work in separate context windows, keeping the main session focused and enabling parallel work. They share the same models and the same permissions — the benefit is isolation, not capability or privilege.

Automating the quality gate

To have tests run before work is declared done, encode the requirement in the project instructions or enforce it with hooks. Relying on the agent to remember is not a mechanism.

Headless use in CI

Running agentic coding unattended in CI demands scoped permissions, no direct push to the main branch, and changes landing as diffs a human reviews. Auto-merging anything green removes the review that made it safe; running as repository admin gives the widest possible blast radius.

A safe CI setup
trigger      pull request only
permissions  read repo, write branch; never push to main
scope        lint and formatting paths only
verify       full test suite must pass
output       PR diff for human review, no auto-merge
Key takeaways
  • Commit project instructions so conventions apply to everyone and stay reviewable.
  • Plan, review the plan, then execute in steps with tests between.
  • State the allowed scope explicitly and ask for the minimal diff.
  • Subagents buy context isolation and parallelism, not extra privilege.
  • Encode the test requirement in instructions or hooks, not in trust.
  • In CI: scoped permissions, no push to main, human-reviewed diffs.
Common pitfalls

Starting on the least understood part of a legacy codebase. Begin where tests make correctness verifiable quickly.

Letting it run unattended overnight. Unreviewed volume is not progress.

At architect level, prompting is contract design. The question is not how to phrase a request but what interface each step exposes to the next, and how that interface is enforced.

Evaluator-optimizer loop — trades tokens for quality, use where it's worth it.

Contract first

Define the schema, constrain generation to it, and validate downstream anyway. On current models that means structured outputs — a schema through output_config.format, or a tool with a strict input schema. Reverse-engineering a contract from observed output is fragile, and free-form text with a regex parser is the pattern this replaces.

Outdated technique

Older material teaches prefilling the assistant turn with { to force JSON. Current Claude models reject a prefilled final assistant turn with a 400 error.

Shape is not meaning

A schema-constrained step can return structurally valid output containing a nonsensical value — an end date before a start date, a negative quantity. That is the mechanism working as specified. Semantic validation stays your responsibility, and returning a clear, actionable error lets the model correct itself on the next turn.

Examples carry what schemas cannot

Schemas express structure; they cannot express convention or judgment about edge cases. One or two worked examples showing the structure filled in — particularly for awkward inputs — communicate expectations a schema has no way to encode.

Prompts as shared infrastructure

When forty prompts must share a tone or policy, copy-paste guarantees the copies drift. Use a shared, versioned system-prompt component included by all of them. Evolving a prompt many systems depend on means versioning it, running the change against a regression set, and rolling out behind a gate — not editing in place and waiting for complaints.

Serving humans and machines at once

When a task must produce prose for people and fields for a system, define one schema containing both rather than generating twice or parsing prose after the fact. One generation, both consumers, guaranteed consistent.

One contract, two consumers
{
  "risk_level": "high",          // for routing logic
  "confidence": 0.82,            // for thresholding
  "summary": "...",              // for the human reviewer
  "evidence": ["...", "..."]     // for audit
}

Generated once against a single schema, so the prose and the fields can never disagree.

Key takeaways
  • Define the schema first, constrain generation to it, validate anyway.
  • Structured outputs replace prefilling, which errors on current models.
  • Schemas guarantee shape, never semantics.
  • Return actionable errors so the model can self-correct next turn.
  • Examples encode conventions and edge cases that schemas cannot.
  • Share one versioned prompt component rather than forty copies.
Common pitfalls

Asking for 'mostly JSON'. Not a contract anything can depend on.

Loosening a schema so it stops failing. That widens the range of bad input rather than fixing the cause.

🎯 Exam Tip — Few-Shot Example Anchor

Providing 1-3 worked examples (few-shot prompting) is the single most effective way to pin down complex output structure across diverse edge cases.

Tools are the agent's interface to the world, and their design determines how often it does the right thing. A tool an agent calls unsupervised must be easy to select correctly, hard to misuse, and clear when it fails.

Fewer, sharper tools beat many overlapping ones.

Few, distinct, well described

Prefer a small number of well-named tools with distinct purposes and strict schemas over many overlapping micro-tools. Descriptions should state when a tool applies and when it does not — selection errors are usually description problems. A generic do-anything endpoint destroys the model's ability to choose correctly, and terse names strip out the information it chooses on.

Protect the context window

A tool that can return ten thousand rows when the agent needs a handful should support filtering and pagination and return concise results. Filtering at the source beats paying to carry data into context and then discarding it. Failing hard above an arbitrary limit makes the tool unusable for legitimate queries; returning a bare file path just moves the work elsewhere.

Design for safe failure

Validate semantics inside the tool and return errors the model can act on. For irreversible external actions, require explicit confirmation and make the operation idempotent or safely retryable where possible, so a retry after an ambiguous timeout cannot double-apply it.

When MCP earns its place

Wrap a capability as an MCP server when multiple clients or agents should reuse it through a standard interface. With one permanent consumer the indirection may not pay for itself, and a protocol hop will not beat an in-process call on latency.

Least privilege at the server

A server exposing SQL for analytics should offer read-only access to a replica, query allowlists and limits, and audit logging. Not production read-write, and never root credentials — the model being careful is not a security control. Descriptions supplied by a third-party server are untrusted content and must not be able to escalate what the agent may do.

Two designs for the same capability
Weak:   run_sql(query)             // full access, unbounded result
Better: search_orders(customer_id, status?, since?, limit=20)
        - read-only replica
        - allowlisted columns
        - paginated, capped
        - documented: when to use, when not to
Key takeaways
  • Few distinct tools with strict schemas beat many overlapping ones.
  • Descriptions must say when a tool applies and when it does not.
  • Support filtering and pagination; protect the context window at the source.
  • Confirm irreversible actions; make them idempotent where possible.
  • MCP pays off when several clients reuse the capability.
  • Least privilege at the server: read-only replicas, allowlists, audit logs.
Common pitfalls

Deleting a tool to fix mis-selection. Sharpen both descriptions instead — that is where the ambiguity lives.

Trusting a connected server's descriptions. Permissions are enforced by your application, not by what a description claims.

Context is the scarcest resource in a long-running agent, and reliability is mostly the discipline of deciding what survives. Everything competes for the same window: instructions, tool results, retrieved material, and the record of what has already been decided.

Compact before context erosion causes forgotten constraints, not after.

Compaction over truncation

As a run grows, early constraints get crowded out. Compaction periodically summarises decisions and state into a durable note that is re-injected as the working record. Blind truncation discards by position rather than importance, so it drops whatever happens to be oldest — often the constraints that mattered most. Compact proactively at a utilisation threshold, leaving headroom to perform the summarisation itself.

Just-in-time retrieval

When a corpus far exceeds the window and most content is irrelevant per query, retrieve rather than preload. Preloading is only sensible when the material is small enough that selecting from it costs more than carrying it.

Keep provenance separate

Distinguish retrieved facts from the agent's own conclusions. Conflating sourced material with generated inference makes errors impossible to trace, and when two sources disagree the conflict should be surfaced with both attached rather than resolved silently by recency.

Deterministic work belongs in code

Date arithmetic, exact totals, identifier validation — let the model orchestrate and let code compute. Instructions cannot make arithmetic deterministic.

Designing for failure

Model outages and degraded responses are routine at scale. Plan fallbacks: retries with backoff, model fallback tiers, circuit breakers, and graceful degradation paths. Add repeated-failure detection with a cap and a defined escalation so an agent cannot repeat a failing action indefinitely.

Measuring reliability

The metric that matters is the rate of runs reaching a correct, verifiable end state, with partial progress tracked separately. Token counts, tool-call volume, and wall-clock time are diagnostics, not goals.

What survives compaction
KEEP    the goal, hard constraints, decisions taken and why,
        open questions, identifiers and references
DROP    verbatim tool output already summarised,
        superseded drafts, exploratory dead ends
NEVER   silently drop a constraint because it was oldest
Key takeaways
  • Compact by importance; truncation discards by position.
  • Compact proactively with headroom to perform the summarisation.
  • Retrieve just in time when the corpus dwarfs the window.
  • Keep sourced facts distinct from generated conclusions.
  • Put deterministic computation in code, not in instructions.
  • Measure verified end-state success, not tokens or step counts.
Common pitfalls

Passing whole transcripts between agents. Pass distilled structured artifacts; raw history is what makes costs explode.

Waiting for a window failure before compacting. By then there is no room to compact.

🎯 Exam Tip — Proactive Compaction

Compact conversation history proactively at a token threshold (e.g. 80% of window) to leave headroom for the compaction call. Waiting for a context overflow failure leaves no room.
